title: Structure and General Properties of the Nonmetals
lead: The nonmetals are taken together: how they bond with metals and with one another, the oxidation states they show and the patterns of their oxidation-reduction chemistry and their oxides, and then the structures of the elements themselves, with the allotropes of carbon, phosphorus and sulfur.
objectives: Describe structure and properties of nonmetals
summary_html: Nonmetals have structures that are very different from those of the metals, primarily because they have greater electronegativity and electrons that are more tightly bound to individual atoms. Most nonmetal oxides are acid anhydrides, meaning that they react with water to form acidic solutions. Molecular structures are common for most of the nonmetals, and several have multiple allotropes with varying physical properties.

exercises.prompt: Carbon forms a number of allotropes, two of which are graphite and diamond. Silicon has a diamond structure. Why is there no allotrope of silicon with a graphite structure?

answer.solution: Silicon has no graphite allotrope because silicon atoms do not form stable π bonds to one another. A graphite layer needs more than σ bonds: each carbon atom uses sp2 hybrid orbitals for σ bonds to three neighbors in a plane, and its unhybridized p orbital, perpendicular to the layer, overlaps side by side with those on adjacent atoms to form π bonds. Good side-by-side overlap requires small atoms, and the first member of each group forms π bonds far more readily than the heavier members. Carbon, the first member of group 14, is small enough, but silicon is much larger, so its 3p orbitals overlap poorly and Si–Si π bonds are weak. Silicon instead uses all four valence electrons in σ bonds, each atom sp3 hybridized and bonded to four neighbors at the corners of a tetrahedron, which is the diamond structure.

exercises.prompt: Nitrogen in the atmosphere exists as very stable diatomic molecules. Why does phosphorus form less stable P<sub>4</sub> molecules instead of P<sub>2</sub> molecules?

answer.solution: In the N<sub>2</sub> molecule, the nitrogen atoms have an σ bond and two π bonds holding the two atoms together. The presence of three strong bonds makes N<sub>2</sub> a very stable molecule. Phosphorus is a third-period element, and as such, does not form π bonds efficiently; therefore, it must fulfill its bonding requirement by forming three σ bonds.

exercises.prompt:
Determine the oxidation number of each element in each of the following compounds:
(a) HCN
(b) OF2
(c) AsCl3

answer.solution: (a) H = 1+, C = 2+, and N = 3−; (b) O = 2+ and F = 1−; (c) As = 3+ and Cl = 1−

exercises.prompt: Arrange the following in order of increasing electronegativity: F; Cl; O; and S.
Why does white phosphorus consist of tetrahedral P<sub>4</sub> molecules while nitrogen consists of diatomic N<sub>2</sub> molecules?

answer.solution: Each group 15 atom has five valence electrons and needs three bonds to complete its octet; nitrogen can make all three to one partner, while phosphorus cannot. Nitrogen, the small first member of the group, forms strong π bonds, so two nitrogen atoms share three pairs of electrons in a triple bond, one σ bond and two π bonds, and the small molecule N2, with one lone pair on each atom, satisfies both atoms. Phosphorus is a larger third-period atom whose 3p orbitals overlap poorly side by side, so P–P π bonds are weak and a P≡P triple bond is not stable. A phosphorus atom must make its three bonds as σ bonds to three different phosphorus atoms. In the P4 tetrahedron each atom sits at a corner, bonded by single bonds to the other three and keeping one lone pair, so every atom has an octet without any π bonding.
